issues.legal_issue: Enclosing a verandah warrants eviction for material alteration only when the landlord proves that the tenant made the alteration without consent and that it materially impaired the premises’ value or utility; the impairment cannot be presumed from the alteration alone.
material_facts: The tenant enclosed the shop’s verandah by building walls on its sides and installing a rolling shutter at the front, and removed the original door.
The alteration was made without the landlord’s consent, and the fact-finder’s conclusion that the tenant made it was not disturbed.
The landlord presented no evidence that the alteration damaged the shop, removed fixtures, or reduced the flow of light or air.
The rolling shutter would ordinarily remain open during the day, and enclosing the verandah increased the shop’s area and did not establish reduced value or utility.
issues.conclusion: The landlord did not prove material impairment, so the alteration did not justify eviction. The High Court correctly rejected eviction on this ground, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires acts by the tenant that are likely to impair materially the value or utility of the premises. The landlord bears the burden of proving the tenant made the construction, did so without consent, and materially affected the premises; these conditions are cumulative. Material impairment is assessed from the landlord’s point of view and depends on proved facts; it is not presumed merely because an addition or alteration was made. Om Prakash v. Amar Singh sets out the cumulative conditions; Brijendra Nath Bhargava v. Harsh Wardhan places the burden of proving material impairment on the landlord and requires a substantial or significant change; Om Pal v. Anand Swamp emphasizes that the question depends on the facts and circumstances. Vipin Kumar v. Roshal Lal Anand illustrates impairment supported by proof that fixtures were removed and light and air were blocked, while Gurbachan Singh v. Shivalak Rubber Industries confirms that the effect must be judged on the proved facts from the landlord’s perspective.

rule.if: material_alteration_eviction_appeal and tenant_made_alteration and alteration_without_consent and not landlord_proved_material_impairment

predicates.material_alteration_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning eviction sought on the ground that a tenant’s alteration materially impaired the premises.
predicates.tenant_made_alteration: The tenant made an alteration to the rented premises.
predicates.alteration_without_consent: The tenant made the alteration without the landlord’s consent.
predicates.landlord_proved_material_impairment: The landlord proved that the alteration materially impaired the premises’ value or utility.
predicates.eviction_on_alteration_ground_not_warran: Eviction is not warranted on the ground of material impairment by alteration.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns eviction for a tenant’s alteration, the tenant made it without consent, and the landlord did not prove material impairment, eviction on that ground is not warranted.
